transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Start: 16:00 PT
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (CS), Daniel, Maya, Rafael (Gridline)

Summary:
Ethan opened with a short orientation to Redwood's hosted conversation generation APIs (chat + text gen), Priya demoed a live console + API call showing streaming and non-streaming behavior, and then we moved into parameter tuning (temp/top_p/max_tokens), batching and retry/backoff patterns for production. Gridline asked about latency SLAs, cost tradeoffs, and data residency; we scoped a POC and agreed next steps.

Topics covered:
- Streaming vs non-streamed responses and when to pick each
- Key generation params and safety of deterministic outputs
- Retry strategies (idempotency, exponential backoff, client vs server retries)
- Console: token breakdown, per-request timing, and the Optimize suggestions pane
- When to consider Dedicated capacity or Private deployment for residency

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ethan from Redwood, I'll kick things off. Quick intro — Priya's our solutions engineer, she'll take the demo, Jordan from CS is here to help with onboarding details.
[00:12] Daniel: Thanks, Ethan. We got about 45 minutes, we wanted to see a practical demo — especially streaming and how retries should work. We run conversational assistants across web + mobile so latency is sensitive.
[00:22] Priya: Great, yeah I'll jump into the console and then show an API call. Quick note: we'll show both streaming (server-sent events) and full-response modes so you can see differences.
[00:34] Rafael: Cool. Also curious about cost impact when we crank down latency.
[00:38] Priya: Totally. Alright I'm sharing my screen — console -> generation -> chat example. I'll kick off a simple prompt about product release notes so you can watch token streaming.
[00:51] [00:51] Priya: Starting stream now... (typing) — you should see chunks come in every ~200-600ms depending on the model and prefix cache hit
[01:05] Maya: I see pieces coming in, sometimes a gap then a burst — is that normal?
[01:09] Priya: Yes, that's the KV cache/hit behavior, and also batching windows on the server. If multiple requests arrive close together they're batched to increase throughput which can add ms. If you need low jitter we show options to prefer latency (smaller batch windows) at higher cost.
[01:26] Ethan: Important callout: batching reduces cost but can increase tail latency. We surface a per-route latency/cost tradeoff in Optimize.
[01:35] Rafael: How do you recommend setting parameters for multi-turn chat? We worry about repetition and hallucination.
[01:41] Priya: For multi-turn, a common pattern is temperature 0.2-0.6, top_p 0.8, and a max_tokens cap per reply. Also use system prompts and structure responses with JSON schema constraints or function/tool calling to reduce hallucinations. We demoed that in other calls but can show quickly.
[01:58] [02:02] Priya: Now a non-streamed example — single request, returns full content when done. This is simpler for some backends but you sacrifice progressive render.
[02:15] Daniel: About retries — if a streaming response fails mid-stream, what do you advise?
[02:21] Priya: Two patterns: client-side restart with idempotency keys, or server fallbacks. In hosted mode we recommend: 1) use an idempotency key per user turn so you can safely re-request; 2) exponential backoff with jitter: e.g., base 200ms, multiplier 2, max 5 retries; 3) detect partial-output and either stitch or restart from last confirmed token depending on your UX needs.
[02:45] Maya: Partial-output stitching seems tricky. Any examples?
[02:49] Priya: Yeah it's fiddly. For chat we often have the client buffer tokens and only commit them once a stable checkpoint comes in. Otherwise, easiest is to re-run the prompt but include last saved reply as context and dedupe on your side.
[03:06] [03:09] Ethan: Also pointer: we provide an SDK helper that handles idempotency and checkpointing patterns — small wrapper for streaming reconnects. I'll share that.
[03:16] Rafael: Does Redwood expose token-level timing so we can measure where buckets of latency happen?
[03:21] Priya: Yes, Console traces per-token breakdowns: model compute vs network vs batching wait. We also export traces to your tracing system via a webhook for long-term analysis.
[03:33] Daniel: On dedicated vs hosted — our legal team cares about data residency and audit logs. What options do we have?
[03:40] Ethan: For residency and stricter SLAs, Dedicated or Private (VPC/on-prem) is typical. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput; Private gives you a customer-managed control plane for stricter network constraints. Both support KMS, audit logs, and SSO.
[03:56] Maya: Any latency SLO numbers? We target p95 < 300ms for short replies.
[04:02] Priya: On hosted shared tier p95 depends on model and length; small models often hit sub-200ms p95 for short prompts. For stricter SLOs we recommend Dedicated where you can size instances, and we can run a short benchmark to validate.
[04:17] [04:20] Daniel: OK. Can we get a benchmark that mimics our traffic (mostly 2–4 token replies but high QPS)?
[04:26] Ethan: Yes — that's part of the POC scope. We'll bring a bench script that replicates QPS and token distribution. Priya will include sample config.
[04:34] Rafael: How about safety/filters? We need blocklist/hard filters for PII leakage.
[04:40] Priya: We have content moderation hooks and allow you to run post-generation checks. For PII we recommend redaction routines server-side and using our streaming hooks to detect sensitive entities as tokens arrive. Not perfect, but combined with auditing it's workable.
[04:59] Maya: Regarding cost, are there levers beyond batch windows and quantization?
[05:04] Priya: Yes: model selection, sequence length caps, prefix caching (reuse KV cache across similar prompts), and dynamic routing to cheaper model variants for non-critical traffic. Optimize provides recommendations and a simulation mode to estimate cost impact when you change settings.
[05:23] [05:27] Priya: I'm going to show an API curl example for streaming. (type) You can see headers: idempotency-key, model, max_tokens, temperature, and stream=true. If the connection drops the SDK can reconnect and resume with the same idempotency key.
[05:41] Daniel: Are retries safe with streaming tokens already delivered to the client?
[05:44] Priya: Depends. If you already rendered partial tokens to end-users, you risk duplication. Best practice: show a typing indicator until the server signals completion or checkpoint. If you have to retry, you either stitch carefully (dedupe) or re-run with the previous final token as part of the prompt.
[06:05] Rafael: How about backoff parameters — what's Redwood's default?
[06:09] Priya: Our sample defaults: initial 200ms, multiplier 2, jitter 0.1–0.3, max retries 5. We can tune for your traffic.
[06:20] [06:23] Ethan: Quick question from our side for infra — any strict egress/firewall constraints we should know about for the POC?
[06:29] Daniel: We do allow outbound but we need to go through a proxy that filters TLS, it'll likely terminate certs. That's a constraint.
[06:35] Priya: Good to know — for Private we can offer a connector pattern to avoid MITM proxies; for hosted we can support proxy compat but may need certificate pinning workarounds. We'll get network team involved on the POC kickoff.
[06:48] Maya: Does the console let us replay traces and regenerate with different params?
[06:52] Priya: Yes — you can open a trace, tweak temperature/max_tokens, and replay to compare outputs and cost. It's handy for prompt tuning.
[07:03] Rafael: Any real examples of using function/tool calls to reduce hallucination?
[07:07] Priya: Yep — we show structured tool calls where the model returns a JSON payload that maps to a backend action. That reduces free-text hallucination because the response must match schema.
[07:18] [07:22] Daniel: About tokenization differences across models — do we need to normalize?
[07:26] Priya: Good point. Tokenization affects cost estimates. We can provide a tokenizer tool in the bench scripts so the POC uses the same token accounting as production.
[07:35] Ethan: Time check — 20 minutes left, want to walk through a short failure-mode demo?
[07:40] Rafael: Yes please.
[07:42] Priya: Alright, I'll simulate a stream interruption at ~60% of the reply and show the two recovery patterns: restart with idempotency key (server dedupe) and client stitch.
[07:55] [07:55] Priya: Simulating drop... now.
[08:03] Maya: We saw a gap then repeats — that looks messy.
[08:07] Priya: Right — that's why UX matters. In-app it's usually better to keep a temporary buffer until final confirmation.
[08:12] Daniel: For our mobile app we'll want to avoid re-renders; so checkpointing makes sense.
[08:16] Priya: Agreed. We'll share the SDK example for incremental commits.
[08:22] [08:25] Rafael: Any limits on idempotency key storage? We have millions of users.
[08:28] Priya: No hard limit — keys are light. If you need long-term retention for dedupe beyond our retention window we can design a sync strategy. We'll discuss during POC.
[08:40] Ethan: Two quick notes — one on telemetry: we provide token-level cost attribution per route; second on fallbacks: you can route to a cheaper model variant when load is high.
[08:53] Priya: Also mention prewarm/burst for Dedicated; if you expect periodic spikes we recommend a small reserved buffer.
[09:00] [09:03] Daniel: Anything else on security? SSO/SAML and audit log formats?
[09:07] Ethan: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs in both Dedicated and Private. Hosted has shorter retention by default but enterprise add-ons extend retention and SOC2/ISO docs are available. I'll send the link.
[09:19] Maya: Can you include sample SAML metadata and an example audit payload?
[09:22] Ethan: Yes, will add to the security pack.
[09:26] Rafael: So next steps: POC bench, security docs, pricing.
[09:31] Ethan: Correct. We'll follow up with dates for the kickoff.
[09:34] [09:35] Priya: Quick final demo note — in the console Optimize tab you'll see suggested batch and cache settings when you upload a sample workload. That often immediately drops estimated cost 10–30% in our customers.
[09:50] Daniel: Love to see the bench numbers reflecting our short reply distributions.
[09:54] Ethan: We'll aim for that. Anything else?
[09:58] Maya: No, that's it from us. Thanks.
[10:00] Ethan: Great, thanks all — we'll email the materials and schedule.
